title: When the Weather Turns
premise: Zephyrine Ashgrove has spent seven years writing postcards to her twin brother, Zephyr, whose name was erased from the family after the fire that took the house — and, she believes, his life. At their mother's funeral, a stranger named Corliss recognizes the twins by their childhood surname, Vane, and reveals that Zephyr did not die in the fire: he survived, changed his identity, and has been living under another name ever since. As Zephyrine and Corliss trace him through the coastal towns he passed through, she must decide whether the brother who abandoned his own name deserves the goodbye she has been rehearsing for years. The novel ends at a hospice bed, where Zephyrine finally speaks his old name aloud; he answers to it once before dying, and she burns the last unsent postcard, choosing memory over correspondence.
about_author: Ivo Voss is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing unclaimed letters in a municipal dead-letter office. They write quiet novels about people haunted by the things they never said, and live near a coastline that appears in most of their work.

chapters.title: The Smile That Ends Conversations
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. Days before her mother's funeral, we see her ritual: postcards addressed to a burned-down house, written in a voice she pretends is her brother's. Her practiced smile deflects every condolence. Emotional beat: grief so managed it has become performance, and the first hairline crack when a mourner mentions 'the Vane girl.'

chapters.title: A Stranger Knows the Old Name
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. At the funeral, Corliss — a weathered man with a fisherman's gait — uses the surname Vane, which no one has spoken since the fire. He claims he knew Zephyr alive, two years ago, working boats up the coast. Emotional beat: vertigo; the ground of Zephyrine's seven-year mourning shifts beneath her.

chapters.title: What the Fire Left Out
chapters.summary: Corliss's POV. He explains how he met a quiet deckhand called 'Fen' whose burn scars matched a story everyone in his hometown knew. He never connected it until today. Zephyrine accuses him of cruelty or fraud; he offers only an address where Fen was last seen. Emotional beat: suspicion warring against desperate hope.

chapters.title: Postcards to Ash
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV, intercut with flashbacks to the fire and the family's decision to erase Zephyr's name after what he did that night. We learn the price of survival was exile from his own identity. Emotional beat: the reader learns why the name was buried — and that Zephyrine chose the postcards as a private rebellion.

chapters.title: Northbound
chapters.summary: Dual POV. Zephyrine and Corliss travel the coast following Fen's trail: a landlady, a tattooed forearm in a crew photo, a bar tab signed with a backwards letter. Each stop confirms more and costs Zephyrine more composure. Emotional beat: rising tension — the trail is fresh, but someone else seems to be asking about Fen too.

chapters.title: The Man Who Answers to Nothing
chapters.summary: Fen's POV, unnamed until the final line. He lives carefully, answerable to no history, until he hears someone in town is looking for a man with his scars. He begins packing. Emotional beat: dread and a strange homesickness for a self he destroyed; the chapter's last word is his true name, spoken only in thought.

chapters.title: Justice Outside the Law
chapters.summary: Corliss's POV. The other searcher surfaces: a relative of the man Zephyr wronged the night of the fire, seeking the reckoning the courts never gave. Corliss must choose between protecting the trail and letting justice run its course. Emotional beat: moral pressure tightens; the journey becomes a race with a consequence attached.

chapters.title: Convergence at Salt Hollow
chapters.summary: All three POVs converge on the coastal town where Fen now lives. Zephyrine reaches his door just as the avenger does; a confrontation in the street forces Fen to claim his name publicly to stop violence — the one thing he fled for fifteen years. Emotional beat: climax; identity reclaimed at the worst possible moment.

chapters.title: Goodbye, Properly, Out Loud
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. Injured in the confrontation, Fen/Zephyr is dying in a hospice ward. Siblings speak across fifteen silent years: his reasons, her postcards, the mother's funeral neither could attend together. She says his name aloud; he answers to it. Emotional beat: catharsis — the goodbye she rehearsed for years finally happens.

chapters.title: Return to Sender
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV, weeks later. She stands at the ruins of the old house with the final unsent postcard, reads it once, and burns it in her palm. Corliss waits by the car; life continues without the ritual. Emotional beat: resolution — she stops writing to the dead and starts speaking to the living, carrying both names forward.
